mappings.rationale: Activity by an unexpected but accepted Kubernetes identity is closest to abuse of Valid Accounts.
If enabled, starting a pod from a disallowed image is direct container deployment.
The event proves deployment of a privileged container; ATT&CK T1610 explicitly covers privileged container deployment, while it does not prove a completed host escape.
The event proves deployment with a risky host mount, an attribute explicitly covered by ATT&CK's Deploy Container detection guidance.
The event proves deployment with the host network namespace, which ATT&CK lists as a risky Deploy Container attribute.
The event proves deployment with the host PID namespace, which ATT&CK lists as a risky Deploy Container attribute.
The event proves deployment with a weakened IPC isolation setting; it does not prove a completed host escape.
A NodePort can expose a remote service, but creation alone does not prove adversary use of External Remote Services.
The event proves insecure credential placement, not adversary search or collection of Credentials in Files.
Allowed anonymous Kubernetes API access is an externally reachable remote-service access path.
Kubernetes attach/exec directly invokes commands through the container administration API.

Rejected candidate: port-forward establishes a network tunnel but does not execute a command inside a container, which is the behavior required by T1609. No current ATT&CK Containers technique cleanly covers the event by itself.
Adding an ephemeral container deploys a new container into an existing pod.
Namespace creation alone has no defensible one-to-one ATT&CK Containers behavior.
Placing a pod in kube-system or kube-public can make it resemble a legitimate system resource.

mappings.rule: Service Account Created in Kube Namespace
mappings.rationale: Creating a Kubernetes service account establishes a new cluster identity.
Role modification can add container-cluster permissions, but the same Falco rule also covers deletion, so one technique is not reliable for every match.
Binding cluster-admin adds a high-privilege container cluster role to an identity.
Creating a wildcard role adds broad container-cluster permissions.
Creating a role with write verbs adds persistent cluster permissions.
Creating a role granting pods/exec adds a cluster permission that enables container command execution.
Creating a deployment causes containers to be deployed into the cluster.
Deleting a deployment destroys workload state and can interrupt availability.
A Kubernetes Service is a network abstraction, not the host-level management daemon described by ATT&CK Container Service.
Deleting a Service may interrupt routing, but the event does not cleanly prove Data Destruction or Endpoint Denial of Service.
Generic ConfigMap creation does not identify an adversary behavior without examining its content or consumer.
Deleting configuration data can destroy workload state and availability.
Generic namespace creation is administrative activity with no precise ATT&CK Containers mapping.
Deleting a namespace can recursively destroy the resources and data it contains.
Creating a service account establishes a new identity for cluster access.
Deletion changes an account but does not match ATT&CK's persistence-focused Account Manipulation behavior cleanly.
Creating a role adds container-cluster permissions that can preserve or elevate access.
Role deletion changes permissions but is not the additional-role behavior described by T1098.006.
Creating a ClusterRole adds reusable cluster-wide permissions.
ClusterRole deletion changes permissions but is not necessarily an additional-role persistence action.
Creating a RoleBinding assigns additional cluster permissions to an identity.
Deleting a RoleBinding removes permissions and does not reliably indicate additional-role persistence.
Creating a ClusterRoleBinding grants additional cluster-wide permissions.
Deleting a ClusterRoleBinding removes permissions and is not a clean match for additional-role persistence.
Secret creation uses the Container API but does not itself gather credentials as T1552.007 requires.
Deleting a secret destroys credential data and can disrupt dependent workloads.
Retrieving a Kubernetes Secret through the cluster API is the behavior described by Container API credential access.
An attempted Kubernetes Secret retrieval is attempted credential gathering through the Container API.
The source macro makes this catch-all rule always false and it has no ATT&CK behavior.
If enabled, use of default administrator names is closest to abuse of Default Accounts.

mappings.rule: Ingress Object without TLS Certificate Created
mappings.rationale: An ingress without TLS exposes a remote service, but the configuration alone does not establish adversary use of External Remote Services.

mappings.rule: Untrusted Node Successfully Joined the Cluster
mappings.rationale: If enabled, an untrusted node identity accepted by the cluster is closest to Valid Accounts, but the fit is indirect.

mappings.rule: Untrusted Node Unsuccessfully Tried to Join the Cluster
mappings.rationale: If enabled, attempted use of an untrusted node identity is closest to Valid Accounts, but the fit is indirect.
The source explicitly disables this catch-all debug rule and it has no ATT&CK behavior.
A successful console login through an assumed cloud role is use of a Cloud Account.
A successful non-MFA console login is use of a cloud account without the expected authentication control.
A successful root console login is high-privilege use of a Cloud Account.
Deactivating the root MFA device directly modifies multi-factor authentication.
CreateUser establishes a new Cloud Account.
A group can carry cloud roles, but group creation alone does not prove additional privileges were assigned.
Deleting a group may remove access, but the event does not establish Account Access Removal impact by itself.
Creating an ECS service deploys and maintains containers.
RunTask or StartTask deploys a containerized ECS workload.
Creating a Lambda function establishes serverless code execution capability.

Rejected candidate: T1578.005 covers infrastructure-level compute settings such as quotas, tenant policies, subscriptions, and regions, not modification of an existing Lambda function's code. T1648 also does not cleanly establish this update event as serverless execution without execution context.

Rejected candidate: despite the API name, T1578.005 covers infrastructure-level compute settings such as quotas, tenant policies, subscriptions, and regions, not an existing Lambda function's application/runtime configuration. No current ATT&CK technique cleanly covers the event by itself.
RunInstances creates new cloud virtual-machine instances.
Launching resources outside approved regions is the behavior described by Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions.
Deleting bucket encryption weakens data protection, but the current ATT&CK catalog has no precise one-to-one behavior for this event.
Removing public-access blocks can enable access to cloud storage, but does not itself show that data was accessed.
If enabled, ListBuckets is direct Cloud Storage Object Discovery.
An ACL may enable access to cloud storage, but the event alone does not prove data access.
A bucket policy may enable access to cloud storage, but the event alone does not prove data access.
Creating a trail is normally defensive administration and has no reliable malicious ATT&CK mapping without its configuration.
StopLogging directly disables a cloud audit log.
